messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Contingency and Reserve" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve (0A+0B)
Accepted scope: Contingency on 0A and 0B separately, stated as a percentage with its basis.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- add · contingency / reserve · supported by all · quantity: Claude 30–40% (0A), 35–50% (0B); Gemini 30% / 25%; GPT 30–40% both · cost: Claude $5–27B · confidence: medium (Claude)

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve (0A + 0B): Technical Proposal

**Status:** Round-3 proposal, interim until the cost baseline is frozen.
**Currency:** constant FY2026 USD. Escalation is carried separately and is never included in contingency.

---

## 0. Executive summary

A single contingency percentage per phase is the wrong instrument for this programme. 0A is reversible research. 0B is an irreversible industrial commitment whose cost estimate is presently AACE Class 5 (about −30%/+100%). I propose a **three-layer reserve stack** for each phase:

1. **Project contingency (PC).** Risk-based and bottom-up, held by the project.
2. **Owner reserve (OR).** Held by the owner board, for unknown-unknowns and licensing/policy threats.
3. **Scope reserve.** A pre-agreed descope ladder that is not money, mainly for 0B.

Under D-02 ("stringency follows reversibility"), the **confidence level rises with irreversibility**. 0A is budgeted at P70/P80. 0B is committed at P80/P90 at KDP-0B.

### Headline recommendation

| | 0A (fund now) | 0B: current planning value (Class 5) | 0B: at KDP-0B (Class 3, required) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base estimate (working assumption, §3) | $6.0B (3.5–9.0) | $19B (10–40) | re-estimated at gate |
| **Project contingency, % of base** | **40%** (35–50) → P70 | **50%** (40–65) → P70 | **35%** (30–40) → P80 |
| **Owner reserve, % of base** | **10%** (8–12) → P80 | **18%** (15–20) → P80 | **14%** (10–15) → P90 |
| Total reserve, % of base | 50% | 68% | ~49% |
| PC, $ | $2.4B (1.2–4.5) | $9.5B (4–26) | ~$6.7B on a $19B base |
| OR, $ | $0.6B (0.3–1.1) | $3.4B (1.5–8) | ~$2.7B on a $19B base |
| **Total contingency + reserve, $** | **$3.0B (1.5–5.6)** | **$12.9B (5.5–34)** | ~$9.4B |
| Scope reserve (descope ladder) | ~10% of base | ~25–35% of base | refreshed at gate |
| Funded schedule reserve | 1 mo/yr pre-I&T, 2 mo/yr I&T, backup target | 6 mo per campaign + one 12-month slip in PC | same |

Combined now: about **$16B (7–40B)** of contingency plus reserve. Only the 0A share, about $3B, is a funding requirement under D-01. The 0B figure is a **planning number that must be carried into the economics gate test**. It is not an appropriation.

### Position on the round-2 figures

- **Gemini (30% / 25%).** I disagree. 25% on 0B is below even the Class 4 upper bound and inverts the risk ordering. 0A retires technology risk, but it does not retire the scale-up, fleet production, remote-industrial integration or operations risks that dominate 0B dollars. 25% is acceptable only on recurring tug units #4 and later, and on array hardware whose price range is already in the base.
- **GPT (30–40% for both).** The 0A band is reasonable. A uniform rate is wrong because it ignores estimate maturity and reversibility. It also gives no basis for converting a percentage into a confidence level.
- **Claude (30–40% / 35–50%).** This is the closest to my position. I raise the 0A floor to 35% because 0A is about 70% NRE and one-off pathfinder hardware, historically the highest-growth category. I split 0B into a current Class 5 figure (40–65%) and an at-gate figure (30–40%). Claude's "$5–27B" mixes PC and OR and both phases. My split totals are 0A $1.5–5.6B and 0B $5.5–34B.

---

## 1. Design philosophy (opinionated)

1. **Contingency is computed, not chosen.** Each percentage is the gap between the base estimate and a stated confidence level on a probabilistic S-curve. The percentages above are outputs of §4–§5, and they will be recomputed at each gate.
2. **Confidence follows reversibility (D-02).** For 0A, a cost overrun leads to a pause or replan, so P70 committed and P80 total authority are sufficient. For 0B, an overrun after KDP-0B strands MW-class assets in deep space, so commitment is at P80 and total authority at P90.
3. **Contingency does not fund project-ending outcomes.** If microgravity Fe-Ni metallurgy fails, the response is a gate decision to activate the Earth-supplied fallback. It is not a reserve draw. Sizing reserve to cover a kill-or-pivot event would produce a meaninglessly large number and would hide the real decision.
4. **No hidden contingency, no double counting.** Base estimates must be most-likely values. Separate lines already exist for:
   - spares (bom-0-14),
   - capacity headroom (bom-0-3/0-4, the ~1.33 capacity/contract ratio),
   - the $30–150/W array price range (bom-0-5).

   Contingency must not re-pad these. Any item found carrying "management margin" in its base has it stripped out and moved here.
5. **Separate threats from variance.** Changes outside project control go to OR, not PC. Examples are the ALARP number under D-03, the licensing state, D-04/D-05 re-decisions and launch-market collapse.
6. **For a non-profit, unfunded contingency is fiction.** PC must be cash or legally callable pledges before the work it covers starts (§11).
7. **No rollover from 0A to 0B.** Unused 0A PC returns to the owner. Carrying it forward would bias the KDP-0B decision.
8. **Contingency is measured against one frozen, configuration-controlled baseline.** It is meaningless against a moving or superseded document set.

---

## 2. Reserve architecture

```
             BUDGET AUTHORITY (per phase)
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  OWNER RESERVE (OR)        held: Owner Board  │  ← unknown-unknowns,
 │  0A +10% → P80 | 0B +14–18% → P80/P90         │    licensing/ALARP, policy
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │  PROJECT CONTINGENCY (PC)  held: Programme Mgr│  ← risk register variance,
 │  0A +40% → P70 | 0B +50% now → +35% at gate   │    estimating uncertainty,
 │  (includes funded schedule slip)              │    integration, one slip
 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
 │  BASE ESTIMATE (BE) – most-likely, no padding │  ← sum of bom-0-1…0-16
 │  incl. spares, capacity headroom per items    │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   + SCOPE RESERVE (descope ladder, not money)    ← pre-agreed deletions
   + TECHNICAL MARGINS (mass/power/Δv/life)       ← physical, owned by items
   + SCHEDULE RESERVE (months, windows)           ← costed inside PC
   (ESCALATION: separate line, not reserve)
```

**Release authority**

| Layer | Who draws | Single-draw limit | Conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC | Programme Manager | ≤$10M (0A), ≤$25M (0B) | Must cite a risk-register ID; ≤25% of annual PC allocation without board review |
| PC | Programme Change Board | ≤$100M (0A), ≤$250M (0B) | Above PM limit, or any draw that changes an interface |
| PC (above board limit) / any OR | Owner Board | none | Any requirement change; any OR use; any draw that drops RCR below 1.0 (§10) |

---

- This is why D-01 frames Phase 0 as a capability programme.
- It is also why **the economics gate must compare 0B with contingency against the Earth-supplied fallback with its own contingency**. I recommend 20–25% for the fallback, since it uses launch and commodity metal with mature estimates. Comparing a padded fallback against an unpadded 0B, or the reverse, would corrupt the gate.

---

## 4. Element-level contingency rates and basis

- **Heritage:** new, modified or recurring.
- **Estimate class:** AACE 18R-97 analogue.
- **Primary cost driver.**

The systemic adder covers four things:
- integration of seven remotely operated element types,
- light-time up to ~15 min one-way with no crew intervention,
- correlated common-cause risks (launch price, metallurgy yield, schedule), and
- one funded 12-month slip of the initial deployment, at a standing-army cost of ~$0.7B.

**Correlation.** Element-level P70 deltas are summed rather than combined statistically. Summation overstates the total if risks are independent and understates it under strong positive correlation. Common-cause drivers dominate this programme, so I use summation plus the adder as the planning method. From SRR onward this is replaced by a Monte Carlo cost-risk model with an assumed inter-element correlation of ρ ≈ 0.3–0.5, the commonly used default range when data are absent.

---

## 5. Probabilistic basis: percentages to confidence levels

I model the cost ratio (actual/base) as lognormal, with parameters chosen from estimate class and first-of-kind cost-growth history. Analogues are major NASA science and exploration projects; JWST and MSR are outliers several times above the original estimate.

| Case | Median ratio | σ(ln) | P50 | P70 | P80 | P90 |

| 0A (Class 4–5) | 1.22 | 0.25 | +22% | **+39%** | **+51%** | +68% |
| 0B now (Class 5) | 1.25 | 0.35 | +25% | **+50%** | **+68%** | +96% |
| 0B at KDP-0B (Class 3) | 1.15 | 0.20 | +15% | +30% | **+36%** | **+49%** |

The bottom-up results from §4 (0A: 40%, 0B: 50%) agree with the top-down P70 values. That agreement is the "basis" the accepted scope asks for.

**KDP-0B entry criterion (proposed).** At KDP-0B:
- the 0B base plus PC must achieve a joint cost-and-schedule confidence (JCL) of ≥80% on an independently estimated Class 3 basis, and
- base plus PC plus OR must achieve ≥90%.

If that requires PC above 45%, it indicates insufficient risk retirement in 0A. The gate should then fail or re-scope rather than pile on reserve.

---

## 6. Where I disagree with round-2, and why

| Model | Round-2 | My view | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gemini | 0A 30%, 0B 25% | 0A 40%, 0B 50% now / 35% at gate | 25% sits at the Class 3 upper bound for a Class 5 estimate. 0B's largest elements (plant, tug fleet, launch) carry scale-up and production risk that 0A does not retire. A lower 0B rate is defensible only after 0A delivers TRL 6 and a Class 3 estimate, and even then P80 lands near 35%. |
| GPT | 30–40% both | Split by phase and by time | A uniform rate ignores reversibility (D-02) and maturity. 30% for 0A would be below my bottom-up 39%. |

| All | Single % | Three-layer stack plus scope reserve | A single percentage blurs who can spend it and on what. Licensing and ALARP threats (D-03) should not be spendable by the project. |

---

## 7. Schedule reserve

Schedule reserve is costed within PC because slip cost is mostly standing army.

**Window physics drives this.** Low-Δv NEAs sit close to Earth's orbit and so have long synodic periods. At a = 1.1 AU (T = 1.154 yr), S = 1/(1 − 1/T) ≈ **7.5 yr**. At a = 1.3 AU, S ≈ 3.1 yr. Low-thrust EP stretches the launch period by months, not years. A missed window therefore costs far more than "months".

**0A requirements**
- Funded margin: 1 month per year to the start of I&T, 2 months per year during I&T, and at least 3 months at the launch site.
- **Backup target required.** The pathfinder must hold a qualified alternate NEA with a departure opportunity within 24 months of the primary.
- If no alternate exists, PC must include an 18–24-month standing-army slip, about $0.6–0.9B at ~$0.35–0.5B/yr. That is roughly the entire integration adder or more. This makes it cheaper to fund target diversity in bom-0-1.

**0B requirements**
- 6 months of funded margin per deployment campaign.
- One 12-month slip of plant deployment funded in PC (~$0.7B at ~$0.6–1.0B/yr burn).
- In steady state the tug fleet buffers missed departures. A single tug miss costs one batch (~150–300 t) of delayed delivery, not fleet idling. That cost is covered by bom-0-3/0-4 capacity headroom, not by PC.

---

## 8. Technical margin policy (interface requirement)

These margins are owned by the items. bom-0-17 sets them as programme-level policy so that cost contingency is not consumed covering missing physical margin.

| Parameter | SRR | PDR | CDR | At launch / gate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dry-mass growth allowance (new design) | 30% | 20% | 10% | 5% system margin vs launch capability | AIAA S-120A-style categories; modified heritage −10 pts |
| EOL power margin (arrays, site and tug) | 25% | 20% | 15% | 10% | Degradation is modelled separately, not in margin |
| Δv | +10% over computed, plus navigation allowance | same | +5% | +5% | Low-thrust trajectories re-optimised per window |
| Propellant | +5% of load, plus residuals | | | | Iodine/argon per D-05 |
| EP thruster life | ≥2× mission throughput by analysis | | ≥1.5× by test | ≥1.5× demonstrated | Life test is a KDP-0B TRL-6 item |
| Heat rejection (radiators) | +20% capacity | +15% | +10% | +10% | Standard temperature margins on top |
| Comms link | ≥3 dB | | | ≥3 dB | |
| Robot battery (10–50 kWh) | safe-mode ≥ 2× worst-case tether-loss recovery time | | | | |
| Product capacity / contract | ≥1.33 | | | ≥1.33 | Consistent with GPT 0.67–1.33 / 0.6–1.0 |

**Rule:** if a margin falls below its floor, the owning item must restore it by design. It may not draw PC unless the CCB approves a margin-recovery draw tied to a risk ID.

---

## 9. Scope reserve (descope ladder)

The descope ladder is agreed in advance, so decisions under pressure are fast and protect the critical tests.

**0A ladder (~$0.6B, ~10% of base)**
1. Reduce scouts from 6 to 4, keeping at least one per candidate spectral class. Saves ~$0.15–0.25B.
2. Drop secondary pathfinder product-handling demos. Saves ~$0.1–0.3B.
3. Defer the receiving-node study detail. Saves ~$0.03B.

**Untouchable in 0A:** every test needed to bring project-ending technologies to TRL 6 for KDP-0B. These are what 0A exists to buy.

**0B ladder (~$5–6.5B, ~25–35% of base)**
1. Defer the water pilot. Saves $0.4B base plus $0.3B PC; it is already conditional.

## 5. Risk-analysis method

### 5.1 Integrated cost and schedule model

Use an integrated stochastic model containing:

- Work-package cost uncertainty.
- Discrete risk events.
- Schedule dependencies.
- Resource-constrained critical paths.
- Delivery opportunities and transport timing.
- Correlations and common-cause failures.
- Decision branches for target rejection, redesign or termination.

Cost uncertainty should not be represented only by independent triangular distributions. That approach tends to understate shared risks.

Examples of important dependencies:

- Target properties affect excavation, recovery yield and equipment wear.
- Process performance affects power, radiator sizing and production rate.
- EP performance affects propellant demand, payload fraction and delivery cadence.
- Common software or manufacturing defects affect multiple robots or tugs.
- Launch delays can affect commissioning, operations cost and delivery dates simultaneously.

### 5.2 Statistical performance requirements

Recommended analytical requirements:

- At least **10,000 simulated programme outcomes** for routine updates.
- Increase runs until reported decision percentiles are stable; target **less than 1% movement** in the reported P80 cost under additional sampling.
- Report P50 and P80 cost, schedule and joint outcomes.
- Report the probability of programme termination separately.
- Test sensitivity to correlation assumptions and tail-event treatment.
- Independently review model structure before KDP-0B.

The intended funding criterion is:

\[
P(C\leq F \;\land\; T\leq D)\geq 0.80
\]

where \(F\) is the funding envelope and \(D\) the approved delivery date.

Two separate P80 results—one for cost and one for date—do **not** establish 80% joint confidence.

Some outcomes should terminate or redirect the programme rather than generate an arbitrarily large contingency requirement.

Examples:

- No suitable target is confirmed.
- Native/reduced Fe-Ni processing fails to meet product requirements.
- Licensing cannot be obtained.
- Phase 1 does not provide signed demand.
- Industrial economics fail the approved decision criterion.
- A project-ending technology fails the mandatory TRL 6 requirement.

For these cases, report:

1. Probability of reaching the gate.
2. Expenditure to the gate.
3. Bounded safe-shutdown or preservation cost.
4. Consequences for Phase 1 procurement.

Earth-supplied material is the fallback planning case, not an unlimited reserve-funded continuation of asteroid industrialization.

---

## 6. Phase-specific risk priorities

### 6.1 Phase 0A

Reserve priorities should be:

1. Representative-material testing and target characterization.
2. Repeated microgravity processing experiments.
3. Integrated power, thermal and containment testing.
4. Autonomous excavation and anchoring demonstrations.
5. EP life testing and propellant qualification.
6. Recovery from a failed or inconclusive pathfinder.
7. Additional regulatory evidence and environmental modelling.

A second demonstration opportunity may be prudent, but a **planned** second article belongs in the base estimate. Reserve covers an unplanned repeat or recovery within the approved demonstration strategy.

### 6.2 Phase 0B

Dominant uncertainties include:

| Risk | Principal consequence | Reserve treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Recoverable metal fraction below expectation | Lower production; more processing time | Model yield, energy and operating-cost effects together |
| Abrasive or adhesive feedstock behaviour | Wear and downtime | Link to maintenance and replacement assumptions |
| Metallurgy or product-quality shortfall | Rework, rejection or failure to qualify | Do not assume reserve can rescue an unproven process |
| Tug availability below prediction | Missed delivery cadence | Model fleet-level reliability and common causes |
| EP propellant qualification or supply disruption | Redesign, procurement delay | Maintain iodine-reference/argon-alternate scenarios |
| Array or radiator growth | Mass, launch and integration cost growth | Propagate through the physical design |
| Licence conditions tighten | Design changes or reduced operations | Include bounded compliance scenarios; preserve stop option |
| Receiving-node delay | Product storage and transport disruption | Model jointly with Phase 1 |

The economics gate should use **delivered, accepted product**, not extracted material or nameplate plant output.

---

## 7. Schedule reserve

Schedule reserve must be stated in time as well as money.

For initial scenario analysis, test:

- **0A:** a recoverable **6–12-month** extension.
- **0B:** a **12–24-month** commissioning or ramp-up delay.

These are stress-test ranges, not approved schedule allowances. The final values must follow the critical path, launch availability and target-specific transport opportunities.

For each delay scenario:

\[
C_{\text{delay}}=
C_{\text{staff retention}}
+C_{\text{operations}}
+C_{\text{supplier extension}}
+C_{\text{storage}}
+C_{\text{revalidation}}
+C_{\text{logistics change}}
\]

Do not apply the programme’s average monthly expenditure indiscriminately. A commissioning delay does not necessarily repeat hardware purchases, while a missed transport opportunity may trigger costs disproportionate to the delay duration.

---

## 8. Autonomy, control and communications requirements

### 8.1 Financial control remains human-authorized

No autonomous spacecraft or production controller may authorize financial reserve expenditure.

Automated systems may:

- Detect performance deviations.
- Forecast maintenance or replacement needs.
- Estimate likely effects on throughput.
- Generate evidence for a change request.

They must not change the approved production commitment or initiate unbounded procurement.

### 8.2 Proposed release authority

| Reserve action | Minimum approval |
|---|---|
| Draw up to 1% of the phase base, within approved scope | Project manager and independent cost-control concurrence |
| Draw above 1% and up to 3% of phase base | Programme change-control board |
| Draw above 3%, or with material architecture/interface effects | Owner approval |
| Any gate waiver or prohibited scope expansion | Not permitted through reserve release |

Every draw must include:

- Risk or change identifier.
- Technical justification.
- Alternatives considered.
- Cost and schedule effect.
- Revised estimate at completion.
- Remaining risk exposure.
- Required configuration changes.

Monthly reporting should show commitments, expenditure, forecast exposure and remaining reserve separately.

### 8.3 Operational data interfaces

Use existing communications and ground-segment services; no separate spacecraft communications network is required.

Necessary evidence includes:

- Equipment duty cycles and degradation.
- Actual process yield.
- Product rejection and rework rates.
- Power and thermal performance.
- Propellant consumption and thruster condition.
- Failures, recovery time and maintenance interventions.

Operational communications latency must not prevent safe local shutdown. That autonomy belongs in the relevant equipment specifications, not in this reserve line.

---

## 9. Manufacturing and procurement considerations

Reserve management should reflect how failures propagate through production.

### Recommended procurement approach

- Qualify first articles before committing the full industrial batch.
- Use staged purchase options rather than unconditional fleet orders.
- Preserve supplier traceability and configuration records.
- Distinguish random unit failure from batch-wide defects.
- Identify long-lead replacement bottlenecks.
- Carry contractual pricing and schedule exposure explicitly.

For example, a manufacturing defect common to multiple tug propulsion units cannot be modelled as independent failure probabilities for every tug. It may require inspection, rework or replacement across a batch.

Base-budget spares remain under bom-0-14. Reserve should not duplicate them. It should address departures from the assumptions used to size those spares.

The personnel, tools and independent reviews needed to operate this control system belong under organizational infrastructure and relevant NRE lines. Their recurring costs should not be charged to the reserve principal.

---

## 10. Development roadmap and readiness

| Milestone | Required reserve-management deliverable |
|---|---|
| **0A authorization** | Separate 0A base and reserve; preliminary conditional 0B provision |
| **Early 0A** | Risk taxonomy, linked cost/schedule model, supplier and launch estimate reconciliation |
| **Internal TRL 4–5 milestones** | Updated uncertainty distributions using measured evidence |
| **Integrated pathfinder review** | Demonstrated yield, reliability, autonomy and thermal-performance inputs |
| **Pre-KDP-0B** | Independent estimate; correlated risk analysis; contractual exposure review |
| **KDP-0B** | Demand-sized baseline; funded reserve; approved schedule; all mandatory gates passed |
| **0B deployment and commissioning** | Monthly controls, quarterly model updates and staged reserve release |

The reserve-control process itself is not usefully assigned a spacecraft TRL.

Under D-02, **every project-ending technology must reach TRL 6 in a relevant environment before KDP-0B, without waivers**. Additional money is not equivalent to technical readiness.

---

## 11. Reserve consumption and warning thresholds

Reserve adequacy should be assessed against **remaining risk**, not merely percentage spent.

Proposed review triggers:

- More than **20% of initial reserve consumed before preliminary design review**.
- More than **40% consumed before critical design review**.
- Remaining reserve below the modelled cost of remaining uncertainty.
- A single risk capable of consuming more than **25% of remaining reserve**.
- Forecast delivery outside the approved joint-confidence envelope.
- A critical technology’s readiness evidence becomes invalid after redesign.

These trigger independent review and possible replanning, not automatic cancellation.

Reserve should be released only when the underlying risk is demonstrably retired. Passing a calendar milestone is not sufficient.

---

## 12. Open engineering and programme questions

Before adopting final dollar values, Project Dyson must resolve:

1. **What are the reconciled 0A and 0B bases?**  
   The reserve cannot be priced credibly until all sixteen other items have consistent boundaries.

2. **What delivery specification will Phase 1 sign?**  
   Quantity, alloy composition, impurity limits, physical form, acceptance testing, location and delivery dates materially affect uncertainty.

3. **What constitutes acceptable relevant-environment evidence?**  
   Especially for microgravity excavation, feed handling, metallurgy and long-duration containment.

4. **How representative are terrestrial test materials?**  
   Laboratory success may not adequately characterize actual target variability.

5. **Which EP propellant and supply chain will be selected?**  
   Continue costing iodine as reference and argon as alternate; retain water EP only as the conditional desk study specified in D-05.

6. **What debris and contamination ceiling will be licensed?**  
   D-03 remains interim. Reserve is not permission to operate above the eventual requirement.

7. **Will SEL1 remain the receiving location?**  
   D-04 is the reference case, not an irrevocable decision.

8. **What is the bounded closeout obligation after a failed gate?**  
   Include spacecraft safing, tracking, disposal or preservation, contractual termination and data retention.

9. **How will Earth-supplied fallback material be financed?**  
   It should be a separately approved Phase 1 procurement decision, not hidden inside asteroid-processing contingency.

---

## Final recommendation

Adopt **35–40% for funded 0A** and **40–50% for the current conditional 0B planning estimate**, both applied to clearly defined, contingency-free phase bases.

Re-estimate 0B at KDP-0B using measured performance, signed demand, supplier evidence and an integrated cost-and-schedule model. Do not promise a lower percentage in advance.

The most important reserve is the ability to **stop before industrial commitment**. Phase 0A should purchase evidence; bom-0-17 should protect that evidence-gathering programme from ordinary uncertainty—not finance an attempt to overcome a failed fundamental premise.

## Key Specifications

- **All three reject the round-2 Gemini figure of 25% for 0B.** Every model now places current-maturity 0B reserve at 40% or more:
  - Claude: project contingency 50% (range 40–65) plus 18% owner reserve.
  - Gemini: 45% (range 40–50).
  - GPT: 40–50% total.

  The shared reasoning is that 0A does not retire the risks that dominate 0B dollars. These are scale-up, fleet production, coupled mining/metallurgy/power/thermal/EP logistics, and long-duration remote operations.
- **0A reserve converges near 35–40% at the project level.**
  - Claude: 40% project contingency (range 35–50), the P70 level.
  - Gemini: 35% (range 30–40).
  - GPT: 35–40% total.

  All three move to or above the upper half of the round-2 "30–40%" band. The reason given is that 0A is dominated by NRE and first-of-kind pathfinder work.
- **0A and 0B use separate ledgers.**
  - Only 0A reserve is a current funding requirement under D-01.
  - The 0B figure is a planning provision carried into the economics gate, not an appropriation.
  - Claude and GPT explicitly forbid using 0B allowances as informal 0A money. Claude also forbids rolling unused 0A contingency into 0B.
- **About 10% of base sits at a higher authority than the project manager.**
  - Claude: owner reserve of 10% (0A) and 14–18% (0B).
  - Gemini: 10% Board strategic reserve in 0B.
  - GPT: 10% programme management reserve in both phases.

  Exogenous threats are routed to this higher layer: licensing and the D-03 ALARP outcome, launch-provider failure, and policy changes.
- **Release authority is tiered, and every draw needs a documented risk or change ID.**
  - Claude: project manager up to $10M (0A) or $25M (0B); change board up to $100M or $250M; Owner Board above that and for any owner-reserve use.
  - Gemini: subsystem, then project, then Board.
  - GPT: up to 1% of phase base, then up to 3%, then owner approval.
- **Three buffers are kept separate:** financial reserve, schedule reserve and engineering margin. Mass, power, Δv and radiator margins are physical. Money cannot create radiator area after deployment. Schedule slips are costed mainly as standing-army burn.
- **Reserve is a pure financial line.** It has no flight mass, power, thermal load or staff. Analysts, cost-risk tools and independent cost estimates are charged elsewhere:
  - Claude places them in bom-0-7, at about $5–15M/yr.
  - GPT places them in bom-0-7 or the NRE lines.
  - Gemini is silent on this.
- **The 0B percentage must be re-estimated at KDP-0B** using pathfinder-measured yield, reliability and supplier evidence, with an independent cost estimate. None of the three treat today's 0B figure as final.

## Divergent Views

- **0B reserve at the KDP-0B gate:** Claude recommends a pre-stated drop to 35% project contingency (range 30–40, the P80 level) plus 14% owner reserve, to reach P90 once the estimate reaches AACE Class 3. Gemini prefers holding 40–50% at the KDP-0B gate, drawn down only as operational milestones are met. GPT suggests recalculating from evidence and explicitly refusing to "promise a lower percentage in advance."
- **Reserve layering:** Claude recommends three layers: project contingency, owner reserve, and a non-monetary descope ladder worth about 10% (0A) and 25–35% (0B) of base. Gemini prefers a three-tier money split: 0A is 15% subsystem plus 20% project manager; 0B is 10% subsystem, 25% project manager and 10% Board. GPT suggests exactly two monetary layers in 0A: 25–30% project contingency plus 10% programme reserve. GPT allows "no third automatic owner contingency" stacked above these.
- **Confidence-level basis:** Claude maps percentages to P70/P80/P90 using a lognormal cost-ratio model.
  - 0A uses σ(ln) = 0.25.
  - 0B now uses σ(ln) = 0.35.
  - 0B at gate uses σ(ln) = 0.20.

  The bottom-up element rates are cross-checked against this. Gemini cites NASA NPR 7120.5F norms without stating a confidence level. GPT targets a joint cost-and-schedule P80 (from at least 10,000 runs) but forbids labelling any percentage-derived budget "P80" before that analysis exists.
- **Dollar sizing:**
  - Claude carries working bases of $6.0B for 0A (range 3.5–9.0) and $19B for 0B (range 10–40). This gives reserve of $3.0B for 0A (1.5–5.6) and $12.9B for 0B (5.5–34).
  - Gemini assumes bases of $2.5–4.0B (0A) and $12–18B (0B), for a total reserve of $6.3–9.5B.
  - GPT gives only normalized rates per $1B, plus an illustrative $2B/$20B case totalling $8.7–10.8B.

  Claude and GPT both say the round-2 "$5–27B" figure is not adoptable because it mixes phases and layers.
- **Fundamental technology failure:** Claude recommends treating outright failure of microgravity Fe-Ni metallurgy as a gate decision that triggers the Earth-supplied fallback, not a reserve draw. GPT agrees and adds reporting of gate probability, spend-to-gate and bounded shutdown cost. Gemini lists the fallback pivot as something that "will consume massive schedule and financial reserve."
- **Schedule reserve and margins:**
  - Claude: 1 month per year before I&T and 2 months per year during I&T; a backup NEA with a window within 24 months; one funded 12-month 0B slip (about $0.7B); power EOL margin of 25/20/15/10% across SRR/PDR/CDR/launch; Δv +10%.
  - Gemini: 2 months per year in 0A and 3 months per year in 0B, plus a 12-month window reserve; 30% power margin; Δv +15%.
  - GPT: stress-tests 6–12 months (0A) and 12–24 months (0B) only, with no fixed allowance.

  Claude and Gemini agree on dry-mass growth allowances of 30% at SRR/PDR, 20% at PDR/CDR, and 10% at delivery.

## Open Questions

1. **Reconciled phase bases.** None of the 0A or 0B base estimates is frozen. The three models' working bases differ by up to about 2.4× for 0A. Reserve dollars cannot be fixed until bom-0-1 through bom-0-16 have consistent boundaries and are stripped of duplicate padding.
2. **Correlation and common-cause modelling.** Claude estimates that choosing ρ = 0.3 versus 0.5 moves 0B P80 by 5–8 points. GPT flags batch-wide tug defects and target-property coupling as correlated drivers. Sensitivity runs are needed before SRR.
3. **Standing-army burn rates and the cost of a missed window.**
   - Long synodic periods for low-Δv NEAs (about 7.5 years at a = 1.1 AU) make a missed window disproportionately expensive.
   - Monthly burn rates for 0A and 0B are unknown (raised by Gemini and Claude).
   - It is also unresolved whether a backup target with a window within 24 months is achievable.
4. **Fallback comparator and its financing.** The contingency to carry on the Earth-supplied fallback at the economics gate is undecided. Claude proposes 20–25%. GPT wants the fallback to be a separately approved Phase 1 procurement.
5. **Non-profit funding realism.** Open items are:
   - whether reserve is held as cash, callable pledges or a mix;
   - how in-kind contributions carry default risk (Claude suggests 30–50%);
   - inflation treatment: Claude and GPT keep escalation as a separate line, while Gemini proposes tying 15% of Board reserve to an inflation index.
6. **Exogenous decisions not yet settled.** These are the final D-03 ALARP and licensing ceiling, a possible re-decision of the SEL1 receiving node (D-04), and the iodine/argon choice (D-05). Each could move element rates by about 10–15 points. They need agreed routing to owner reserve versus scope change.

## Recommended Approach

1. **Adopt interim rates on a contingency-free base, in constant FY2026 USD, with escalation carried separately.**
   - 0A: total reserve of 40–50% (point 45%), made up of 35–40% project contingency plus about 10% owner/programme reserve. This sets the funded 0A authority.
   - 0B: total of 55–70% (point about 65%), made up of 45–50% project contingency (range 40–65) plus 15–18% owner reserve. This is recorded only as an uncommitted planning provision.
   - All three models reject the round-2 25% figure for 0B and the uniform 30–40% rate across both phases.
2. **Use two monetary layers plus a non-monetary descope ladder.** Project contingency sits with the programme manager and change board. Owner reserve sits with the Owner Board and covers licensing/ALARP, policy, D-04/D-05 re-decisions and launch-market regime change. Pre-agree descope steps that protect every test needed to reach TRL 6 for KDP-0B. Example 0B steps include:
   - deferring the water pilot;
   - reducing the tug fleet from 14 to 10;
   - shrinking the receiving node to minimum product acceptance.
3. **Make contingency computed, not chosen.**
   - Run a bottom-up element-rate method (TRL/AD², heritage, estimate class) now, cross-checked against a top-down lognormal model.
   - From SRR, replace both with an integrated cost-and-schedule Monte Carlo model that includes explicit correlation and common-cause drivers.
   - Do not label any figure "P80" until that model supports it.
4. **Set the KDP-0B reserve criterion rather than a pre-promised number.**
   - Base plus project contingency must reach at least 80% joint cost-and-schedule confidence on a Class 3 estimate validated by an independent cost estimate.
   - Base plus all reserve must reach at least 90%.
   - If more than about 45% project contingency is needed to get there, the gate fails or is re-scoped. Reserve is not piled on.
5. **Keep project-ending outcomes out of reserve.** These include metallurgy failure, no viable target, no signed demand, no licence, and failed economics. Each is a gate decision. Report its probability, spend-to-gate and bounded safe-shutdown cost. At the economics gate, compare 0B with its contingency against the Earth-supplied fallback with its own contingency (provisionally 20–25%).
6. **Fund schedule reserve explicitly and keep margins with the owning items.**
   - Schedule allowances: 1–2 months per year in 0A, at least 6 months per 0B campaign, and one funded 12-month 0B deployment slip.
   - Require a qualified backup NEA within 24 months, since target diversity is cheaper than funding a slip.
   - Mass-growth policy: 30% at SRR, 20% at PDR, 10% at CDR, and 5% system margin at launch. Power, Δv and radiator margins are set by the owning items.
   - Margin shortfalls are restored by design, not by drawing contingency.
7. **Install governance suited to a non-profit.**
   - Every draw cites a risk ID, with tiered release limits.
   - A Reserve Coverage Ratio below 1.0 triggers a recovery plan within 30 days.
   - Independent review is triggered if more than 20% of reserve is consumed before PDR or more than 40% before CDR.
   - Contingency must be in cash or callable pledges before authority to proceed.
   - No 0A-to-0B rollover is allowed, and all reporting is against the single frozen configuration baseline.
